passage: Monday: Uday held up Pallavi's pencil box in class. "This is so cheap. Mine cost way more." Some kids giggled. Pallavi's face burned, and she wanted the floor to swallow her. Tuesday: at lunch Uday started again about his new bag. Pallavi picked up her tiffin without a word and walked to the other bench, where Rekha and Ishan made room. Friday: on sports day, everyone's parents were on the sidelines except Uday's. He bragged louder than ever, listing things his family owned. Pallavi watched him, and something clicked: he looked like someone who needed to be noticed. She didn't answer him. She turned back to Rekha and Ishan and their game.

qa.q: What did Uday call Pallavi's pencil box?
qa.a: He called it cheap.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when Uday held up her pencil box, and what showed it?
qa.a: She felt ashamed; her face burned and she wanted the floor to swallow her.

qa.q: What choice helped Pallavi handle Uday's bragging, and why?
qa.a: Walking away to the bench with kinder friends worked, because she did not argue and stayed with people who made room for her.

qa.q: How might Uday be feeling on sports day when he brags louder than ever?
qa.a: Possibly insecure or lonely, since his parents were not on the sidelines and he seemed to want attention.

grounding: A child ashamed by a rich classmate's bragging sees that his words reflect his insecurity, not her worth, and stays with kinder friends.

passage: Monday: The trip form came round. Neelam read the amount and folded the paper into her bag. "I don't feel like going," she told her friends, with a laugh that didn't reach her eyes. Her cheeks were hot. Tuesday: she stayed behind at the bell and stood by the teacher's desk, twisting her fingers. "Ms Swati, I can't... my family can't pay for the trip." Ms Swati put her pen down. "Thank you for telling me, Neelam. That takes courage. Let me see what can be done, quietly." Thursday: Ms Swati handed her the form, already filled in. "It's sorted. No one needs to know." Neelam's shoulders loosened. She packed her bag for the trip that night.

qa.q: Where did Neelam put the trip form on Monday?
qa.a: She folded it into her bag.

qa.q: Why did Neelam say she didn't feel like going on the trip?
qa.a: She was embarrassed that her family could not pay, so she hid the real reason behind a laugh, though her hot cheeks gave it away.

qa.q: How did talking privately to Ms Swati help Neelam?
qa.a: It let her share her worry without anyone else knowing, and Ms Swati found quiet help so she could go.

qa.q: How might Ms Swati see Neelam's decision to tell her?
qa.a: As a brave step that deserves thanks, which is why she said it takes courage.

grounding: A child embarrassed that she cannot afford the class trip speaks privately to a teacher who quietly arranges help.

passage: At the school's annual day, the hall was full of parents in good clothes. Elizabeth had come with Anjali Aunty, who helped at home and looked after her when her parents were at work. A visiting relative of another family snapped his fingers at her: "You, hold my bag." Anjali Aunty took it silently. Elizabeth felt her chest tighten. She stood up. "Thank you, Aunty," she said loudly. "Please sit here." Then a girl in a yellow costume waved from the stage and Anjali Aunty's whole face lit up. "That's my daughter," she whispered. Elizabeth grinned. "She's so good! She's Class 4, right?" They clapped together.

qa.q: Whose daughter was in the yellow costume on stage?
qa.a: She was Anjali Aunty's daughter.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth's chest tighten when the visitor snapped his fingers?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair and disrespectful to treat Anjali Aunty like a servant, so she decided to show politeness herself.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth show respect to Anjali Aunty?
qa.a: She thanked her out loud, offered her a seat and took an interest in her daughter on stage. 🙂

qa.q: How might Anjali Aunty have felt when Elizabeth thanked her and asked about her daughter?
qa.a: Seen and valued, which is likely why her face lit up when she whispered that it was her daughter.

grounding: A child shows respect to the household helper when a visitor treats her as lesser, and remembers she is a mother too.

passage: Dear diary, I'm Lalremsiami, and today at the traffic signal a little girl tapped on our car window. She was smaller than me and had no slippers. My chest felt tugged and heavy. I looked at her and wanted to give her everything in my school bag. Shalini didi said not to open the window because the light was about to change. At dinner I asked Papa what I could do that is actually safe and helpful. He said we could keep packets of biscuits in the car to give, and next week we'd look together at a group that helps children like her. I feel a little lighter, but I still keep thinking about her small feet.

qa.q: What did the little girl at the signal not have on her feet?
qa.a: She had no slippers.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she looked at the girl?
qa.a: A heavy tug of compassion, and she wanted to give the girl everything in her school bag.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do that turned her feeling into a safe plan?
qa.a: She asked Papa what she could do that is safe, and they planned to give packets of biscuits and look at a group that helps children. 🙂

qa.q: How might Shalini didi have seen the moment at the signal?
qa.a: She was thinking about safety, as she told Lalremsiami not to open the window because the light was about to change.

grounding: A child feels compassion for a begging child at a signal and asks her parent about safe ways to help.

passage: Lunch-break note, Ms Alka. I noticed Bhupen at the end of the bench with no tiffin today. His friend Yash slid his own box towards him. "Mum packed too much," Yash said, and carried on talking about cricket as if nothing had happened. Bhupen's ears went pink and he stared at the box. He said, "Thanks," softly, took one piece of paratha, and smiled a small, awkward smile. I stayed at my desk and did not step in. The next day Bhupen came with roasted chana in a twist of paper. "Have some," he said. Yash took a big handful and said it was tasty. Both boys looked pleased.

qa.q: What did Bhupen bring the next day?
qa.a: He brought roasted chana in a twist of paper.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when his ears went pink and he stared at the box?
qa.a: Probably awkward and embarrassed at being helped, along with gratitude, since he thanked Yash softly and smiled a small smile.

qa.q: What made it easier for Bhupen to accept Yash's food?
qa.a: Yash did not make a show of it and kept talking about cricket, so Bhupen could accept warmly and later share something of his own. 😊

qa.q: How might Yash have seen the moment when he slid his box over?
qa.a: As something ordinary, since he said Mum packed too much and carried on talking about cricket.

grounding: A child gratefully but awkwardly accepts a richer friend's tiffin and shares something of his own in return.

passage: Monday: At the water tap, three boys copied Eshaan's way of speaking and called him names, laughing. Eshaan stared at the ground. Chinmay saw it from the doorway. Heat rushed to his face; it wasn't right, and he was angry, but he stood frozen. Wednesday: Chinmay picked up his lunchbox and sat next to Eshaan. "Do you like cricket?" he asked. They talked about bowling all through lunch. Eshaan laughed for the first time that week. The following Tuesday: the name-calling started again at the tap. This time Chinmay said quietly to Eshaan, "Come on, let's tell Sir." Together they walked to the staffroom. The teacher put down a pen and listened.

qa.q: Where did the three boys call Eshaan names?
qa.a: At the water tap.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel when he saw the name-calling on Monday?
qa.a: Angry, as shown by the heat in his face, but also frozen and unsure what to do.

qa.q: What steps did Chinmay take that were kind and effective?
qa.a: He sat with Eshaan at lunch, talked about something they both liked, and when the name-calling continued he went with him to tell the teacher.

qa.q: What might it be like for Eshaan when Chinmay sits next to him?
qa.a: It eases his loneliness, and he laughs for the first time that week.

grounding: A child who sees a classmate being called names sits with him and, when it continues, tells a teacher.

passage: Sunday: At the family lunch, Uncle said loudly that people from the next district were not to be trusted. Zubin's parents nodded. So did his aunt. Zubin's stomach twisted, because his best friend Aman was from there. He looked at his plate and said nothing. His cousin Afreen caught his eye and gave a tiny shrug. Monday: at school Zubin passed Aman the ball first, on purpose, and sat next to him. Thursday: Zubin found his grandfather feeding the sparrows. "Dada, why did Uncle say those things?" Dada sighed. "He was cheated once, long ago, and it stuck." Zubin thought about that. "But Aman never cheated anybody," he said. Dada didn't answer, only looked at the sparrows.

qa.q: Who caught Zubin's eye at the family lunch?
qa.a: His cousin Afreen did.

qa.q: Why did Zubin's stomach twist when Uncle spoke?
qa.a: He felt uneasy because his best friend Aman came from the next district, and Uncle's words did not match what he knew of Aman.

qa.q: What did Zubin do that let him hold his own view without a fight?
qa.a: He stayed quietly friendly with Aman at school and later asked his trusted grandfather why Uncle thinks that way.

qa.q: How might Zubin's grandfather see Uncle's opinion?
qa.a: As something that grew from one old bad experience that stuck, rather than something based on everyone from there.

grounding: A child feels uneasy when an elder talks badly about a group and the family nods, and quietly holds his own view before asking a trusted elder.

passage: Trisha, come and sit. I hear someone told you girls can't play cricket. Let me tell you something. I'm Deepika, your Masi. When I was ten I loved cricket. The boys in our lane said, "Girls don't play, go and skip." It felt so unfair that my chest went hot. But I still went every evening with my bat and stood at the edge of the lane. I asked my father why there was such a rule. He said, "It's how it's always been." I said, "That's not a reason." One day a boy called Imran said, "Let her bowl one." Months later, they had stopped saying it. Keep your bat, Trisha.

qa.q: What did the boys in Deepika's lane say to her?
qa.a: They said, "Girls don't play, go and skip."

qa.q: What did ten-year-old Deepika feel when the boys said girls don't play?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair, so much so that her chest went hot.

qa.q: What did Deepika do that Trisha could also do?
qa.a: She kept doing what she loved, turned up every evening, and asked why the rule existed.

qa.q: How did Deepika's father see her question about the rule?
qa.a: He offered no reason beyond how it had always been, which suggests he had not thought about why the rule exists.

grounding: A girl told girls should not play cricket feels it is unfair, keeps playing and asks why the rule exists, told by an elder.

passage: I'm Nilesh. Last Sunday I went to my friend Tarun's house to play. His mother gave the cook, Sunita Aunty, water in an old steel glass that lived on a separate shelf. Nobody else used it. Sunita Aunty didn't say anything and drank it standing near the door. I didn't understand, and my tummy felt heavy and sad. At home that night I asked Papa, "Why does she get a separate glass? Is that fair?" Papa was quiet, then said that people are sometimes treated unfairly and that we should treat everyone the same. Now, when Sunita Aunty comes to our house, I bring her water in a normal glass.

qa.q: Where did the cook's glass live at Tarun's house?
qa.a: It lived on a separate shelf.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when he saw the cook drink from the separate glass?
qa.a: Confused and sad; he did not understand the reason and his tummy felt heavy.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that was a start toward fairness?
qa.a: He asked his father whether it was fair, and now offers Sunita Aunty water in a normal glass.

qa.q: How might Sunita Aunty have felt drinking from the separate glass near the door?
qa.a: Possibly uncomfortable or hurt, since she stayed silent and stood near the door, though we cannot know for sure.

grounding: A child sees a cook made to drink from a separate glass, feels confused and sad, and asks his father about fairness.

passage: In PE class, the teacher told Sumit's group to pick teams. Sumit, who wore a hearing aid and sometimes asked people to repeat things, stood at the side. Kabir whispered, "Don't pick him, he's weird." Two others nodded. Mridul's stomach clenched. He didn't want to be the one to argue, and he was afraid they'd turn on him. He looked at Sumit's face and saw him pretend not to notice. Mridul said nothing, but when it was his turn, he quietly said, "Sumit, come on my side." Kabir rolled his eyes. Mridul kept his gaze on the ball. Sumit walked over and gave him a small nod.

qa.q: What did Sumit wear that made him stand out to the group?
qa.a: He wore a hearing aid.

qa.q: Why did Mridul stay quiet when Kabir whispered, "Don't pick him"?
qa.a: He was afraid to disagree and worried the others would turn on him.

qa.q: What could Mridul do next to keep helping Sumit?
qa.a: He can keep being friendly in small ways, like picking him for his side, and later speak to a teacher if the exclusion goes on.

qa.q: How might Sumit be feeling when he pretends not to notice the whispering?
qa.a: Probably hurt and trying to protect himself, which is why he acted as if he had not heard.

grounding: A child afraid to disagree with friends who exclude a different child stays quietly friendly with him.
